title: What does the song rest on?
hook: three singers sit down to talk shop, and one keeps asking: what holds that up? the answer goes all the way to space
carry: the last ground of everything is brahman
tomorrow: which Veda does Krishna call himself?

segments.voice: Yesterday, still in the Sama Veda: upasana, seeing the whole world in the rite. The Chandogya hears this world, the wind and the moon in the chant's small sounds.

Why is the sky blue? Because of the light. Why? Because of the air. Why? Small children play this at bedtime, and the questions stop only when someone runs out of answers, or patience. The Chandogya Upanishad tells a story that runs like that. Three men skilled in the high chant of the Sama Veda sit down to talk about it, two brahmins and a king. And one question keeps getting asked, each time one step further down: what does that rest on?
screen: `WHY? BECAUSE. WHY?` → `THREE SINGERS SIT DOWN TOGETHER.` → `WHAT HOLDS UP A SONG?`

segments.voice: Their names are Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana. Pravahana, the king, says: you two speak first; I'll listen. So Shilaka asks Dalbhya, in paraphrase: what does the saman, the chant, rest on? Dalbhya says: on tone, the sound of the voice. And tone? On breath. And breath? On food. And food? On water. And water? On that world, the heavens. And the heavens? Here Dalbhya stops. We don't lead the chant past the heavens, he says; we set it there. Shilaka isn't satisfied. The heavens, he says, rest on this world, the earth beneath us. Then Shilaka puts the question to the king: and this world, what does it rest on? Pravahana's answer: on space. All beings come out of space and go back into space, he says. Space is greater than all of them, the last support. Here the teaching opens wide. The Brahma Sutra, the classic summary of the Upanishads, stops at this very passage and asks: what is this space? Its answer, followed by Vedanta's great teachers, Shankara and Ramanuja among them: not empty air. It's Brahman, the one reality all beings come from and go back to, since only Brahman could be the source and end of everything. That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas, arriving in a talk between three singers: under the song, the breath, the food and the earth, there is Brahman. A note only rings because there's room around it. In this teaching, everything rings in Brahman.
screen: `TWO BRAHMINS AND A KING.` · `TONE, BREATH, FOOD, WATER, HEAVEN.` · `AND THE EARTH? IT RESTS ON SPACE.` · `THE BRAHMA SUTRA: THAT SPACE IS BRAHMAN.` · then, large: `UNDER EVERYTHING, BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: At the end of each out-breath there's a small pause before the next breath comes; let your attention rest there without stretching it. Then listen for the quiet between one sound and the next, and the gap after a passing thought, the open room everything else happens in. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, three singers ask what the chant rests on, all the way down to space, which Vedanta reads as Brahman. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the last ground of everything is Brahman. The king called it space. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1278 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHICH VEDA DOES KRISHNA CALL HIMSELF?`

howItsDone: The dialogue of Shilaka, Dalbhya and King Pravahana is taught from the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, as a meditation on the high chant resting finally on space.

fork.setup: Pravahana says all beings come out of space and go back into it. the Brahma Sutra asks: what is that space?
options: just the empty air around us
Brahman, the one reality everything comes from
fork.reveal: Brahman. only Brahman could be the source and end of all beings, so Vedanta's teachers read Pravahana's space as Brahman.

original.note: Sanskrit: space, open room. In Chandogya 1.9 it is the last support of the high chant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song rests on a good voice.
what it means: in the Chandogya, the chant rests on tone, breath, food, water, heaven, earth, and finally space.

what a scholar hears: gati, 'support', asked again and again until Pravahana answers ākāśa, from which all beings arise and into which they return (Chandogya 1.8–1.9); Brahma Sutra 1.1.22, ākāśas tal-liṅgāt, reads that ākāśa as Brahman.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

chat.says: babysitting my little cousin. bedtime = 'what's under the ground? and under THAT?' for 20 min 💀 he wants a real answer. what do i tell him
options: a king in the Chandogya kept going: the earth rests on space, everything comes from it and goes back. Vedanta calls that ground Brahman.
the earth rests on the heavens, and that's where you stop asking.
nothing is under it; Hindus say the question has no answer.
chat.meaning: In Chandogya 1.8–9 the chain goes down past the heavens and the earth to space, from which all beings come and to which they return; the Brahma Sutra reads that space as Brahman.

tie.story: Two singers stopped at the heavens and the earth, and King Pravahana went one step further: everything rests on space.
tie.friend: Priya can tell her cousin that at the bottom of every 'and under that?' Hindus find Brahman, the ground everything comes from.
tie.you: what do you keep asking 'and under that?' about?

Pravahana.meaning: the king who listens first, then answers: space

Shilaka.meaning: a singer who presses the question past the heavens

Dalbhya.meaning: a singer who stops the chain at the heavens

Brahman.meaning: the one reality everything comes from and returns to

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.8 (Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana: the chant rests on tone, breath, food, water, the heavens, the earth)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.9.1–2 (all beings arise from space and return to it; space is the final support; the udgitha is without end)
Brahma Sutra 1.1.22 (ākāśas tal-liṅgāt: the 'space' of Chandogya 1.9.1 is Brahman), with Shankara's and Ramanuja's commentaries

notes: Names given in short form: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, Pravāhaṇa Jaivali; confirm 'two priests and a king' (Pravāhaṇa as a kṣatriya king; the other two as brahmins).

Order of the chain (svara, prāṇa, anna, āpaḥ, 'that world', 'this world', ākāśa) and who says which step are given from memory; confirm. In the text Dālbhya stops at 'that world' and Śilaka names 'this world'.
'Without end' for the udgitha as parovarīyas / ananta in 1.9.2; confirm the paraphrase.
'Sing into a pillow and it dies' is an everyday illustration, not a claim about the text.
